mainTopic: יום טוב שני for one who knows the calendar; punishing רב נתן בר אסיא; and explanations of רבי יהודה's view on moving פירות שביעית
overview: The amud opens by finishing a question about doing מלאכה on יום טוב שני for someone who knows the calendar. רב אמי rules that it is forbidden in a settled area, because of מחלוקת, but permitted in the desert. Next comes a story: רב יוסף punished רב נתן בר אסיא for traveling on the second day of שבועות. In one version he gave נידוי; in the other he gave מלקות. Both versions rely on the practice in ארץ ישראל of flogging a תלמיד חכם rather than excommunicating him. The גמרא then returns to the משנה about carrying פירות שביעית. It asks how רבי יהודה can disagree with the rule that a traveler keeps the strictness of both places. רב שישא answers by moving רבי יהודה's words to a different case, and then, after a challenge, the גמרא reverses the opinions so that רבי יהודה is strict. אביי keeps the text and explains it as a return-trip case, but רב אשי rejects this. רב אשי instead compares the argument to a dispute about three vegetables pickled in one barrel, and רבינא begins comparing it to a dispute about dates in צוער, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Labor on יום טוב שני in the desert
steps.stepSummary: The speaker, who knows the fixed calendar, says he avoids מלאכה on יום טוב שני in a settled area. The reason is to avoid deviating from custom and causing מחלוקת. He asks what the rule is in the desert.
steps.simpleTranslation: In a settled area I do not do labor, because changing from the custom causes dispute. In the desert, what is the rule?
steps.whatsHappening: This finishes a question that began on the previous amud. Someone who knows the real calendar date asks whether he may do מלאכה on יום טוב שני when nobody is around to see.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is not saying יום טוב שני means nothing to him. He is saying that the reason he personally keeps it in town is to avoid standing out against the community, which is the rule of שינוי המחלוקת. So he asks: if that reason is missing, as in an empty desert, does the restriction still apply?

keyTerms.meaning: Deviating from local custom in a way that causes conflict
Desert; an empty area with no community around

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as saying יום טוב שני is optional. The question is only about one specific reason for keeping it, the concern of מחלוקת. It asks what happens when that reason seems not to apply.

phrases.english: In a settled area I do not do [labor]
phrases.notes: Spoken by someone who knows the true calendar date

phrases.english: because of deviation [from custom] that causes dispute.
In the desert, what [is the rule]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a question begun on the previous amud
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is מלאכה on יום טוב שני permitted in the desert, where there is no community to cause מחלוקת with?

steps.title: רב אמי: forbidden in town, permitted in the desert
steps.stepSummary: The answer, quoting רב אמי: in a settled area it is forbidden, and in the desert it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what רב אמי said. In a settled area it is forbidden; in the desert it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The question gets a direct answer, quoted from רב אמי. Where people are around, it is forbidden; in the desert, it is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling follows the reason given in the question. The ban for this person rests on the concern of מחלוקת, so where that concern disappears, the ban is lifted. This is a special exception for someone who knows the calendar. It does not cancel the general practice of יום טוב שני.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא of ארץ ישראל whose ruling is quoted

steps.whatToRemember: Someone who knows the calendar keeps יום טוב שני in a settled area because of מחלוקת. In the desert, רב אמי permits מלאכה.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַב אַמֵּי:
phrases.english: He said to him: Thus said Rav Ami:
In a settled area it is forbidden; in the desert it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַב אַמֵּי
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In a settled area it is forbidden; in the desert it is permitted, because the concern of מחלוקת is absent there.

steps.title: רב נתן בר אסיא travels on the second day of שבועות
steps.stepSummary: רב נתן בר אסיא traveled from רב's yeshiva to פומבדיתא on the second day of שבועות, and רב יוסף put him in שמתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נתן בר אסיא went from the yeshiva to פומבדיתא on the second day of שבועות. רב יוסף excommunicated him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story connected to the topic of יום טוב שני. A scholar traveled outside the תחום on the second day of שבועות, and רב יוסף punished him with שמתא, a form of excommunication.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the person in the desert in Step 2, this scholar broke יום טוב שני publicly, traveling from town to town. That brings back the concern for keeping the custom. The punishment shows how seriously this was taken. This step sets up אביי's question about the type of punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: The scholar who traveled on יום טוב שני
פומבדיתא, a major Babylonian Torah center
עצרת; the Talmud's name for שבועות

phrases.english: Rav Natan bar Asya went
from the study hall to Pumbedita
on the second day of the festival of Atzeret (Shavuot).
phrases.notes: He relied on knowing the true calendar date

phrases.english: Rav Yosef excommunicated him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נָתָן בַּר אָסְיָא אֲזַל מִבֵּי רַב לְפוּמְבְּדִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related story showing how public desecration of יום טוב שני was treated
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Publicly desecrating יום טוב שני is punished; רב יוסף gave שמתא.

steps.title: אביי: why not flog him instead?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רב יוסף why he did not give the scholar מלקות instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Let the Master flog him with lashes!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי questions רב יוסף's choice of punishment. He suggests מלקות (lashes, here the rabbinic מכת מרדות) instead of excommunication.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי assumes that מלקות is the harsher penalty, so it seems the more fitting one for so serious a sin. That is why רב יוסף's answer in the next step begins 'עדיפא עבדי ליה': I actually did something more severe. The challenge is to the choice of punishment, not to whether the act deserved punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: With flogging; the doubled verb stresses the action

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
Let the Master flog him with lashes!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: וּלְנַגְּדֵיהּ מָר נַגֹּידֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the punishment given in Step 3
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Flogging seems to be the harsher penalty and so the fitting one for this grave sin. Why use the apparently lighter excommunication?

steps.title: Excommunication is the harsher punishment for a scholar
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that he punished him more severely. In ארץ ישראל they vote to flog a תלמיד חכם but do not vote to excommunicate him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I did something more severe to him. In ארץ ישראל they vote to flog a Torah scholar, but they do not vote to excommunicate him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף explains that שמתא is actually worse than מלקות. He proves it from the practice in ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sages of ארץ ישראל were willing to flog a scholar but held back from excommunicating him, out of respect for the Torah he carries. That shows שמתא is the harsher penalty. So by excommunicating him, רב יוסף was being stricter, not more lenient.

keyTerms.meaning: Something greater, here a more severe punishment
They vote or take a count, in a בית דין
A yeshiva student, a תלמיד חכם

phrases.english: He said to him: I did something more severe to him,

phrases.aramaic: דִּבְמַעְרְבָא מִימְּנוּ אַנִּגְידָּא דְּבַר בֵּי רַב,
phrases.english: for in the West (Eretz Yisrael) they vote on flogging a Torah scholar,
but they do not vote on excommunication.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: the supposedly lighter punishment is actually heavier
steps.terutzMaskana: For a תלמיד חכם, שמתא is harsher, as the practice in ארץ ישראל shows

steps.title: Second version: רב יוסף flogged him
steps.stepSummary: A second version of the story says רב יוסף flogged רב נתן בר אסיא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב יוסף flogged him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives a different version of the same story. In this version, רב יוסף chose מלקות. This sets up a reversed exchange with אביי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the punishment changes. In this version, the question of which punishment fits will run the other way.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say; it introduces a different version

phrases.english: Some say: Rav Yosef flogged him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different version of the story in Steps 3-5
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, רב יוסף punished with מלקות.

steps.title: אביי: רב and שמואל require excommunication
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks why רב יוסף did not excommunicate him. רב and שמואל both say one gives נידוי for breaking יום טוב שני של גליות.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Let the Master excommunicate him! For רב and שמואל both say that one excommunicates for desecrating the second day of יום טוב in the Diaspora.
steps.whatsHappening: In this version, אביי challenges רב יוסף from the other direction. He cites a ruling of רב and שמואל that the set punishment for this sin is נידוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is now based on a stated source, not just a suggestion. If רב and שמואל fixed נידוי as the punishment, using מלקות seems to go against an established rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The two days of יום טוב kept in the Diaspora

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: Let the Master excommunicate him,
for Rav and Shmuel both say

phrases.aramaic: מְנַדִּין עַל שְׁנֵי יָמִים טוֹבִים שֶׁל גָּלִיּוֹת!
phrases.english: one excommunicates for [desecrating] the second day of Yom Tov of the Diaspora!

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב and שמואל set נידוי as the punishment for breaking יום טוב שני

steps.title: A scholar is spared excommunication for his benefit
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that the rule of רב and שמואל is for an ordinary person. For a תלמיד חכם, flogging is better for him, as the practice in ארץ ישראל shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: That applies to an ordinary person. Here, he is a Torah scholar, so I did what was good for him. In ארץ ישראל they vote to flog a Torah scholar, but they do not vote to excommunicate him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף limits the rule of רב and שמואל to ordinary people. For a scholar, he chose the lighter penalty out of respect for his Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general rule of נידוי still stands. A תלמיד חכם is an exception in how the rule is carried out. Both versions use the same fact from ארץ ישראל, but here it explains why רב יוסף was easier on him, while in the first version it showed he was stricter.
steps.whatToRemember: Both versions agree on one point. נידוי is harsher than מלקות, and a תלמיד חכם is spared נידוי out of respect for Torah.
steps.confusionAlert: Both versions quote the same line about ארץ ישראל for opposite purposes. In version one it shows רב יוסף was stricter; in version two it shows he was gentler.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָנֵי מִילֵּי — אִינִישׁ דְּעָלְמָא.
phrases.english: He said to him: That applies to an ordinary person.
Here, he is a Torah scholar,
so I did what was good for him.

phrases.aramaic: דִּבְמַעְרְבָא מִימְּנוּ אַנִּגְדְּתָא דְּבַר בֵּי רַב,
phrases.english: For in the West they vote on flogging a Torah scholar,
but they do not vote on excommunication.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָנֵי מִילֵּי — אִינִישׁ דְּעָלְמָא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule: an exception for a תלמיד חכם
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone who breaks יום טוב שני gets נידוי
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule of נידוי is for ordinary people; a תלמיד חכם is given מלקות instead, for his own good
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how בית דין adjusts the way a punishment is carried out out of respect for Torah scholars, while the underlying rule stays in place.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה on transporting Sabbatical produce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה: likewise, one who carries פירות שביעית from one place to another.
steps.simpleTranslation: Similarly, one who carries Sabbatical-year produce, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and quotes its next case about פירות שביעית. This line just sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה teaches that someone who moves שביעית produce between places where it has run out in the fields at different times must follow the stricter rule of both places for ביעור. רבי יהודה disagrees, saying he can tell others to go and bring produce from where it is still found.

phrases.aramaic: כַּיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ הַמּוֹלִיךְ פֵּירוֹת שְׁבִיעִית וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: Similarly, one who carries Sabbatical-year produce, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the story to the next clause of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who transports פירות שביעית follows the strictness of both places; רבי יהודה disagrees.

steps.title: Does רבי יהודה reject the rule of both places' stringencies?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבי יהודה does not accept the משנה's general rule that one bears the stringencies of the place he left and the place he went to.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי יהודה not hold of what we learned in the משנה, that we place on him the stringencies of the place he left and the stringencies of the place he went to?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה's lenient view. It seems to go against the משנה's general rule that a traveler keeps the strictness of both places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה earlier stated a general rule about a traveler, and no one there disagreed with it. Yet here רבי יהודה lets him eat the produce, following only the more lenient place. The question is how רבי יהודה can disagree with that basic rule.

keyTerms.meaning: That we learned in a משנה
רבי יהודה, the תנא who is lenient in this case

phrases.english: And does Rabbi Yehuda not hold
that which we learned [in the Mishnah]:

phrases.aramaic: נוֹתְנִין עָלָיו חוּמְרֵי הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁיָּצָא מִשָּׁם
phrases.english: We place upon him the stringencies of the place from which he left
and the stringencies of the place to which he went?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵית לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הָא דִּתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהודה's view in the משנה just quoted
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's lenient ruling on פירות שביעית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's general rule makes a traveler keep the strictness of both places, but רבי יהודה lets him follow only the more lenient place

steps.title: רב שישא: רבי יהודה is discussing a different case
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי answers that רבי יהודה does accept the general rule. He is talking about a separate case: fruit taken from a place where the crop has not run out to another such place, and then the crop runs out back home.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא son of רב אידי said: רבי יהודה is talking about a different case. This is what the משנה means: Or if someone went from a place where the crop has not run out to another place where it has not run out, and then heard that it ran out in his home town, he must remove the fruit. רבי יהודה says: (He can tell the people back home) 'You too, go and bring some for yourself from where I brought them, since there it has not run out.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question of step 10. רבי יהודה does not argue on the general rule; he is speaking about a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this new case, both places still have the crop in the field, but the home town later runs out. The תנא קמא says he must do ביעור because of his home town. רבי יהודה is lenient, because the fruit came from a place where the crop is still growing.

keyTerms.meaning: ran out; the crop is gone from the fields
you too, go and bring for yourself

steps.confusionAlert: In this reading רבי יהודה is the lenient one, and the תנא קמא ("חייב לבער") is the strict one. Hold on to this, because the very next step challenges it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi said:
Rabbi Yehuda is saying a different matter,
and this is what it is saying:
Or, from a place where it has not run out
to a place where it has not run out,
and he heard that it ran out in his home place —
he must remove it.
phrases.notes: This is the view of the תנא קמא in this reading.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Go out and bring for yourself, you too,
from where I brought them,
for there they have not run out.
phrases.notes: So he is lenient: no ביעור needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10 by moving רבי יהודה's statement to a different case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יהודה seemed to reject the rule of following the stringencies of both places.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה agrees to that rule. He speaks about a separate case, where he is lenient because the source place still has the crop.

steps.title: Challenge: רבי יהודה only spoke as a stringency
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב שישא's reading. It makes רבי יהודה lenient, but רבי אלעזר said רבי יהודה only stated his view as a stringency.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that רבי יהודה is speaking to be lenient? But רבי אלעזר said: רבי יהודה said it only to be strict!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 11. A known teaching of רבי אלעזר says רבי יהודה's statement is strict, not lenient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב שישא's reading turned רבי יהודה's words "צא והבא לך" into a leniency. רבי אלעזר's tradition says those words were meant strictly. So the reading of step 11 cannot stand as it is.

keyTerms.meaning: is that to say? (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: Is that to say that Rabbi Yehuda is speaking to be lenient?
But didn't Rabbi Elazar say:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אֶלָּא לְחוּמְרָא!
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said it only to be strict!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב שישא's reading, which makes רבי יהודה lenient.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אלעזר's tradition says רבי יהודה's view is a stringency, which contradicts a lenient reading.

steps.title: Reverse the opinions so רבי יהודה is strict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes רב שישא's reading by swapping the opinions. In the same case, the תנא קמא says no ביעור is needed, and רבי יהודה is strict because the crop ran out where the fruit came from.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, reverse it: He does not need to remove it. רבי יהודה says: (The people can tell him) 'You too, go and bring some from where you brought them,' and there it has run out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by switching who is strict and who is lenient. Now רבי יהודה fits רבי אלעזר's tradition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case stays the same: both places had the crop, and then the home town ran out. Now the תנא קמא is lenient. רבי יהודה is strict, because the place the fruit came from no longer has the crop.
steps.confusionAlert: Only the opinions are swapped; the case is the same as in step 11. Now "וְהָא כָּלוּ לְהוּ" means 'there it HAS run out', the opposite of step 11.

phrases.english: Rather, reverse it —
he is not required to remove it,
Rabbi Yehuda says:
Go out and bring for yourself, you too,
from where they were brought,
and there they have run out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12 by reversing the opinions in רב שישא's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יהודה was the lenient one in this case.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה is the strict one, which matches רבי אלעזר.

steps.title: אביי keeps the text and explains a return-trip case
steps.stepSummary: אביי does not reverse anything. He explains that רבי יהודה's strict view applies when fruit was taken to a place where the crop ran out, and then brought back home where it has not run out.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Really, keep it as it is taught. This is what it means: Or from a place where it has not run out to a place where it has run out, and he brought the fruit back to its home place where it still has not run out — he does not need to remove it. רבי יהודה says: (They can tell him) 'You too, go and bring from where you brought them,' and there it has run out.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a different answer to the question of step 10. He keeps רבי יהודה strict, without swapping anything, by explaining a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In אביי's case, the fruit came home from a place where the crop had already run out. The תנא קמא looks at where the fruit is now, so no ביעור is needed. רבי יהודה looks at the place he just brought it from, where it ran out, so he requires ביעור.

keyTerms.meaning: really, as it is taught (no change to the text)
and he brought them back to their place

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Actually, as it is taught,
and this is what it is saying:
Or, from a place where it has not run out
to a place where it has run out,
and he brought them back to their place
and there it still has not run out —
he is not required to remove it,
Rabbi Yehuda says:
Go out and bring for yourself, you too,
from where they were brought,
and there they have run out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to step 10, instead of רב שישא's answer as fixed in step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the case without changing the text
steps.terutzHavaAmina: To keep רבי יהודה strict, we would need to reverse the opinions.
steps.terutzMaskana: The text stays as is. The case is fruit brought back home from a place where the crop ran out.

steps.title: רב אשי: Did the donkey's back make the fruit forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי attacks אביי's case. The fruit only passed through a place where the crop ran out, carried on a donkey. Why should that make it forbidden?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי challenged this: According to רבי יהודה, did the donkey's back absorb the fruit?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי objects to אביי's explanation from step 14.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In אביי's case, the fruit was not grown in the place where it ran out, and it is not being eaten there. It was only carried through on an animal. It makes no sense for that short stay to make the fruit need ביעור.

keyTerms.meaning: is it as if...? (a rhetorical challenge)
on the back of a donkey

phrases.english: Rav Ashi strongly objected to it:
According to Rabbi Yehuda, is it as if
the donkey's back absorbed them?!

steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's case of fruit brought back home.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Just passing through a place on a donkey should not give the fruit that place's status.

steps.title: רב אשי links the argument to a dispute about pickling
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives his own explanation. The argument in the משנה matches a dispute of תנאים about someone who pickles three kinds of vegetables in one barrel. רבי אלעזר says one may eat them based on the first vegetable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: This is like the argument of these תנאים, as we learned in a משנה: Someone who pickles three kinds of pickles in one barrel — רבי אלעזר says: One may eat them based on the first one.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting אביי, רב אשי offers a new approach. He starts quoting a משנה with a parallel argument, and the quote continues in the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is how to handle produce whose crops run out at different times. Like fruit from different places, the vegetables in one barrel have different end dates. רבי אלעזר says the time is set by the first vegetable, meaning the first one to run out, and then all must be removed.

keyTerms.meaning: תנאים, the sages of the משנה era
as we learned in a משנה

steps.whyThisMatters: רב אשי makes the dispute a general question about mixed produce. It is not tied to one unusual travel case.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:
It is like the dispute of these Tannaim,
as we learned in a mishna:
One who pickles three kinds of pickles in one barrel,
Rabbi Elazar says:
One may eat based on the first.
phrases.notes: One may eat all of them until the first kind runs out in the fields.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דְהָנֵי תַנָּאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's rejected explanation with a new approach based on a parallel dispute of תנאים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Linking the dispute to a parallel argument of תנאים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The argument in the משנה depends on a special travel case, as אביי said.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is the same as the dispute about mixed produce whose crops run out at different times.

steps.title: רבי יהושע: Follow the last vegetable
steps.stepSummary: Continuing the source רב אשי cited, רבי יהושע rules that all three pickled vegetables may be eaten as long as the last one is still in the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע says: You may even keep eating all of them based on the last vegetable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues quoting the source that רב אשי brought. Here רבי יהושע gives the most lenient view: as long as even one vegetable in the barrel is still growing in the field, you may eat all of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier view (step 16) went by the first vegetable to run out, so it was strict. רבי יהושע goes by the last one to run out, so it is lenient. This gives רב אשי his two sides: one view says a little permission permits everything, and the other says a little prohibition forbids everything.

keyTerms.meaning: Even based on the last one, meaning the vegetable that stays in the field longest
Ran out or finished, meaning the crop is no longer found in the field

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse "first" and "last" here. "First" means the first vegetable to disappear from the field, which is the strict view. "Last" means the last vegetable to disappear, which is the lenient view.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says:
Even based on the last one.
phrases.notes: All the vegetables may be eaten until the last kind runs out from the field.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל הָאַחֲרוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the source of תנאים quoted in step 16 by giving the second, lenient opinion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parallel to a dispute of תנאים
steps.terutzMaskana: The lenient תנא קמא matches רבי יהושע's 'last vegetable' view, and the strict רבי יהודה matches the 'first vegetable' view.

steps.title: רבן גמליאל: Each vegetable follows its own kind
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל rules that each vegetable must be removed from the barrel once its own kind runs out in the field, and the הלכה follows him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן גמליאל says: Any vegetable whose kind has run out from the field must be removed from the barrel. The הלכה follows his words.
steps.whatsHappening: The quoted source ends with a third, middle view. רבן גמליאל says each vegetable goes by its own kind, and the source concludes that the הלכה follows him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל does not let the vegetables affect one another. Each one is handled separately: when its kind is gone from the field, that kind is removed from the barrel. This ends the source; רב אשי's parallel rests on the first two views.

keyTerms.meaning: He must remove it (ביעור of שביעית produce)
And the halacha follows his words

steps.whatToRemember: רב אשי's answer: the lenient תנא קמא matches רבי יהושע's 'last vegetable' view, and the strict רבי יהודה matches the 'first vegetable' view. In practice, the הלכה follows רבן גמליאל: each kind goes by itself.

phrases.english: Rabban Gamliel says:
Any one whose kind has run out from the field —
must remove its kind from the barrel,
and the halacha follows his words.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: כׇּל שֶׁכָּלָה מִינוֹ מִן הַשָּׂדֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the quoted source with the third opinion and the practical ruling.
steps.terutzMaskana: The source ends with each kind judged on its own, and the הלכה follows רבן גמליאל.

steps.title: רבינא links the argument to a dispute about dates
steps.stepSummary: רבינא offers a different parallel: the dispute in the משנה matches a dispute about eating dates until the last trees in צוער stop producing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: The argument matches a dispute between these תנאים, as we learned in a משנה: People may eat dates until the last ones in צוער are gone. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says:
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא begins his own explanation, different from רב אשי's. He quotes the first view of a source about dates, and this passage stops just as רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's opposing view is about to begin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dates in צוער ripen last, so the first view lets everyone keep eating dates until צוער's dates run out. In that view, one place where the crop still exists permits the fruit elsewhere. רבינא will show that the opposing view of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל matches the other side of the argument in the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: תנאים, the Sages of the משנה era
As we learned in a משנה
צוער, a town whose date palms produce the latest fruit

phrases.english: Ravina said:
It is like the dispute of these tanna'im,
as we learned: One may eat dates
until the last ones in Tzoar run out.
phrases.notes: צוער's dates are the last to ripen, so they are the last to disappear.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
phrases.notes: His opinion continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a new parallel instead of רב אשי's pickled-vegetables parallel.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parallel to a different dispute of תנאים
steps.terutzMaskana: Not finished yet. The opening view lets dates be eaten everywhere until the last ones in צוער run out, and the opposing view continues on the next amud.
